latin.2390: THESIS I. JUXTA communem Doctorum Scholae Reformatae sensum Gratia ut plurimum designat ipsum Dei amorem & favorem quo nos immerentes prosequitur, aliquando vero etiam quaedam ejus dona & effecta creata. Sic Tilenus thesibus de variis divinae voluntatis nominibus disputatione prima thesi 20. docet Dei gratiam sumi active & passive. Ac prior, inquit, significatio benignam & propensam Dei voluntatem omnia liberaliter & gratis, non ex merito nostro, vel ex debito, imo largientem. Posterior donum aliquod gratis datum declarat.
latin.2391: II. Et ita quoque Petrus Martyr in locis communibus, Nomen, inquit, gratiae in sacra scriptura bifariam accipitur. Primum quidem & praecipue significat Dei erga homines benevolentiam & gratuitum favorem quo prosequitur Electos. Deinde quia Deus Electos suos praeclaris donis afficit, gratia interdum significat ea etiam dona quae nobis a Deo gratis conferuntur. Classe 3. loco 2. paragr. 7.
latin.2392: III. Similiter Aretius in locis communibus loco vigesimo quinto docet sacras literas, quum de gratia loquuntur, primo hac voce intelligere gratuitam Dei misericordiam qua se manifestat in hominis reconciliatione & justificatione. Deinde per gratiam significare quoque dona Spiritus sancti, quae dona ibidem agnoscit recte dici posse gratiam infusam. Et eodem recidit distinctio Polani. Gratia Dei, inquit, ὁμωνύμως dicitur, Est enim vel in Deo residens, vel a Deo data. In Syntagmate Theologiae Christianae parte 1. lib. 2. cap. 21.
latin.2393: IV. Quamvis autem Theologi Reformati agnoscant per Dei gratiam in scriptura sacra quandoque designari divini favoris & amoris erga nos munera & effecta, paucis tamen in locis gratiam eo sensu sumendam esse putant. Siquidem omnia illa loca ubi dicimur per Dei gratiam electi, vocati, justificati, servati, contendunt minime exponenda esse de dono aliquo nobis inhaerente, sed tantum de gratuito Dei amore & benevolentia. Uti praesertim apud Polanum videre est. Gratia, inquit, Deo gratum atque acceptum faciens, atque ita & gratia salvans, qua sumus electi in Christo ad salutem aeternam, efficaciter vocati, justificati, regenerati, qua denique aeternum servamur, non est qualitas nobis infusa, non aliquid in nobis creatum & inhaerens, non charitas qua nos Deum diligimus, aut ulla alia virtus in nobis. Syntagmatis Theologici lib. 2. cap. 21. modo citato.
latin.2394: V. Porro quum gratia sumitur pro divini favoris donis atque effectis observat Tilenus illam communi quadam significatione ipsam naturam, & illius dotes & munera complecti, proprie tamen restringi ad dona quaedam supernaturalia hominibus a Deo concessa. Quae dona rursus vult duorum esse generum. Quaedam enim proprie & directe spectare salutem ejus qui recipit, ut effecta gratiae illius activae qua nos Deus justificat: Qualia sunt fides & charitas & spes. Alia vero non tam pertinere ad peculiarem eorum quibus dantur salutem, quam ad communem totius Ecclesiae usum & aedificationem: qualia sunt donum prophetiae, linguarum & miraculorum & ii quae sunt ejusmodi.
latin.2395: VI. Eodem redit quod docet Zanchius libro quarto de Natura Dei cap. 2. quaest. 1. Scilicet ea Dei dona quae nomine gratiae aliquando significantur, vel ad vitam aeternam pertinere, uti sunt fides, spes & charitas, & quae cum iis conjunctae sunt virtutes: vel non pertinere ad vitam aeternam, uti donum linguarum, miraculorum, & alia de quibus Paulus 1 Cor. 12. Quibus similia legere est apud Polanum loco praeallegato.
latin.2396: VII. Neque multum abludit distinctio Cameronis tomo primo praelectionum digressione de gratia, ubi dicit gratiae dona quaedam esse quae nullis contingunt, qui iidem non servantur: alia vero quae illis etiam obtingunt qui non servantur. Item Dei dona dividi in ea quae aliis tantum, non etiam nobis prosunt, qualia sunt omnia Dei dona in impios collata: & ea dona quae saepe aliis prosunt, aliquando non prosunt, semper tamen iis prosunt in quos sunt collata, qualia sunt fides, spes, & charitas.
latin.2397: VIII. Istae vero donorum gratiae divisiones apud Reformatos receptae parum aut nihil differunt a solenni apud Scholasticos gratiae divisione in gratiam gratis datam & gratiam gratum facientem: ut agnoscit Tilenus ante citata disputatione prima de variis divinae voluntatis nominibus thesi 22. Sed tamen Theologi Reformati plerique istam Scholae Romanae distinctionem carpunt & reprehendunt. Et primo quidem iis displicet quod quaedam Dei dona specialiter dicantur gratia gratis data: quia nulla est gratia quae non gratis donetur. Nec minus gratuita Dei dona sunt spes, fides & charitas, quam donum prophetiae, sanationum & similia.
latin.2398: IX. Deinde iis non probatur quod quidquam in nobis creatum & inhaerens dicatur gratia Deo gratum atque acceptum faciens, ut videre est apud Polanum Aretium & Petrum Martyrem locis supra citatis. Non quod negent Dei dona, quae Scholae Rom. Doctores per gratiam gratum facientem designant, esse aliquid Deo placens, quo Deus delectetur, & quod ipsi gratum sit: Sed quod istis donis non primum Dei favor hominibus conciliatur; cum ipsa sint effecta favoris & amoris divini, & procedant a Deo nobis favente, nosque diligente, etiam antequam illa acceperimus: juxta illud Joannis, Non quod dilexerimus Deum, sed quia prior ipse dilexit nos.
latin.2399: X. Hanc autem esse Doctorum illorum sententiam patet ex ipsorum verbis. Sic enim Petrus Martyr in locis communibus Classe tertia loco secundo numero octavo de gratia infusa Scholasticorum loquens, Non est, inquit, parvus error quod volunt nos hoc habitu, seu creatura reddi gratos Deo. Necessarium enim est, cum ille nos hujusmodi dono affecerit, eum nos amasse prius. Amor enim Dei praecedit omnia ejus dona: Et numero decimo tertio. Nec minus errant, inquit, qui garriunt in scholis, aliam esse gratiam gratis datam, aliam gratum facientem. Omnem enim gratiam oportet gratis dari. Nam alioqui, ut Paulus ait, non esset gratia. Cumque per gratiam gratum facientem intelligant habitum, ut supra docuimus, male statuunt homines per ejusmodi dona apud Deum gratos effici. Nam apud eum per solam ejus misericordiam, & propter Christum recipimur in gratiam.
latin.2400: XI. Et similiter Camero in jam supra memorata digressione de gratia, Caeterum, inquit, observandum est dona Dei nunquam dici hoc sensu gratiam, quasi iis conciliaretur Dei favor, eaque dona nos redderent Deo gratos & acceptos. Sed si quando dona Dei dicuntur gratia hoc sensu, hominum ratio habetur, qui istis donis inducuntur in amorem, non autem habetur ratio Dei. Quod ut percipiatur intelligendum est humanum amorem qui conciliatur istis donis, non efficere haec dona, sed invenire. At amor divinus idem invenit & effecit haec dona: ut pictor qui delectatur opere suo, idem gaudet pulchritudine operis, & autor fuit istius pulchritudinis. Itaque nulla debuit dici gratia gratum faciens proprie loquendo, sed potius dicenda fuit illa gratia gratum facientis.
latin.2401: XII. Unde patet Doctores Reformatos non negare fidem, spem, charitatem, & similia Spiritus Sancti dona esse res Deo gratas, & quarum ratione homo, in quo reperiuntur, Deo placeat & gratus sit: sed tantum ista dona non praevenire Dei favorem & benevolentiam erga nos, verum ejus esse effecta & munera.
latin.2402: XIII. Porro Tilenus hac in parte non videtur aliud in Scholasticis reprehendere, quam quod dona illa quae vocant gratiam gratum facientem, confundant cum gratia justificante & salvante, quae ex Theologorum Reformatorum sententia, non est aliquid in nobis inhaerens, sed tantum gratia Dei activa & externa. Loquens enim de spe, fide & charitate, Hanc gratiam, inquit, gratum facientem vocant Scholastici, & cum illa ἐνεργητικῇ periculosissime confundunt. Thesi illa 22. saepius citatae disputationis de variis divinae voluntatis nominibus.
latin.2403: XIV. Nonnulli quoque ex Scholae Reformatae Doctoribus distinctionem gratiae in gratis datam & gratum facientem admittunt quidem, sed alio sensu, quam qui apud Scholasticos Doctores receptus est. Nam Testardus in Irenico per gratiam gratis datam intelligit eam per quam Deus hominem ad salutem invitat: per gratiam vero gratum facientem, illam per quam Deus hominem efficaciter immutat, convertit atque sanctificat. Vel gratia gratis data ipsi genus quoddam est; gratia vero gratum faciens ea generis illius species per quam homini fides ingeneratur, peccata remittuntur, sanctitas infunditur. Ut videre est thesi trecentesima. Distinctio, inquit, gratiae in gratis datam, & gratum facientem sic potest admitti, ut gratis data dicatur ea quae tantum praevenit invitando a parte Dei, qualis est generalis: gratum faciens, quae etiam gratis data est, sed hominem efficaciter immutando, de abominando facit Deo gratum & acceptum. Vel ut gratia gratis data sit genus gratiae generalissimum & omnem gratiam significet; gratia vero gratum faciens sit gratiae gratis datae species ea, qua fidem ingenerat, peccata remittit, sanctificat, subjectum uno verbo praeparat.
latin.2404: XV. Rivetus autem in summa controversiarum tractatu quarto quaestione secunda, per gratiam gratis datam intelligit omnia dona gratiae; per gratiam vero gratum facientem, quam etiam gratis dantem vocat, intelligi vult ipsum Dei favorem, a quo dona illa procedunt. Quo sensu Paulus Ferrius in specimine Scholastici orthodoxi capite trigesimo, distinctionem eandem usurpat. Nam per gratiam gratum facientem significat gratiam Deo immanentem, quae non ponit aliquid circa gratificatum, sed est ipse Dei amor: sub gratia vero gratis data comprehendit omnia beneficia vocationis, justificationis, &c. ex gratia gratis dante, tanquam ex fonte uberrimo in nos dimanantia.
latin.2405: XVI. Porro apud plerosque Doctores Reformatos non reperitur expresse posita gratiae distinctio in actualem & habitualem. Imo videntur illam repudiare vetustiores quidam ex Reformatis. Nam Petrus Martyr loco supra citato ex professo refutat sententiam Scholasticorum, qui finxerunt, ut ait, gratiam esse habitum infusum in animam. Sed recentiores Scholae Reformatae Doctores, ut etiam veteres plerique, agnoscunt dari quandam gratiam habitualem. Nam de virtutibus Theologicis loquuntur ut de habitibus divinitus infusis. Et Robertus Baronius Scotus Theologiae in Academia Abredonensi professor testatur hac in parte Modernorum, ut loquitur, Theologorum consensum esse unanimem. Atque etiam hanc de gratia habituali sententiam prolixe adversus Grevinchovium tuetur Gulielmus Amesius in rescriptione ad responsum Nicolai Grevinchovii capite decimo.
latin.2406: XVII. Imo illos ipsos ex vetustioribus qui dissentire videntur, revera non dissentire puto. Quum enim contra Scholasticos contendunt gratiam non esse habitum in animam infusum, manifeste de gratia justificante agunt. Itaque mens eorum simpliciter non est, nullos habitus virtutum in fidelium animas a Deo per Spiritum sanctum infundi, & ejusmodi habitus nullibi gratiae nomine designari: sed hoc tantum, gratiam per quam in scripturis dicimur servari & justificari, in sanctis istis habitibus nullo modo consistere: sed per gratiam istam unice significari Dei misericordiam & benevolentiam. Cujus rei argumentum est, quod aliquando gratiam qua servamur, justificamur, imo & regeneramur, non tantum negant esse habitum & qualitatem infusam, sed quicquam in nobis creatum & inhaerens, uti de Polano supra retulimus. Et tamen idem Polanus in eodem capite agnoscit esse quandam gratiam inhaerentem, quae, inquit, est tum fides, tum gratia conversionis & regenerationis, quam gratiam Christi Redemptoris, item gratiam Christianam vocant. Adeoque quum negat gratiam regenerantem esse quicquam in nobis creatum & inhaerens, loquitur tantum de causa efficiente & impulsiva regenerationis nostrae, non de causa quam vocant Scholastici formalem.
latin.2407: XVIII. An autem praeter habitus virtutum detur gratia quaedam habitualis immediate ipsam animae essentiam penetrans atque afficiens, ut ex Scholasticis multi opinantur, res est de qua expresse non agunt plerique Scholae Reformatae doctores, sed a qua non multum abesse videtur, esse illud novum & supernaturale, & habitualis omnium facultatum innovatio, quam in regeneratione homini tribui agnoscunt. Paulus tamen Ferrius Pastor Ecclesiae Metensis nuper in Domino defunctus diserte ejusmodi quandam gratiam admittit. Et censet ante ipsum conversionis actum, a Deo in ipsam substantiam animae infundi habitualem quandam gratiam, quae totam animam instar spiritualis cujusdam lucis penetrat, & ex animae substantia in omnes ejus facultates sese insinuat: Et sic eas praeparat ut ductum gratiae efficacis sequantur, eique facile & sponte pareant, ut videre est in homilia illa quam publice edidit in Heb. 12. 28. Verum hanc sententiam pluribus scio non placere.
latin.2408: XIX. Distinctio gratiae in excitantem atque adjuvantem, non ita frequens est in Schola Reformata, ut in Schola Romana. Ejus tamen meminit, eamque probare videtur in citata modo homilia doctissimus ille Ferrius. Et ea quoque utuntur in Synodo Dordracena Theologi Britanni.
latin.2409: XX. Caeterum non improbant Scholae Reformatae Doctores quod Scholastici gratiam distinguunt in Operantem & cooperantem. Sed cum Thomistis recentioribus per gratiam Operantem intelligi volunt illam per quam aliquis primum ad Deum convertitur: per cooperantem vero illam per quam aliquis jam ad Deum conversus ad bene agendum movetur. Sic Aretius loco supra citato, Gratia, inquit, alias est operans, alias cooperans. Illa dicitur voluntatem nostram sanare & mutare in melius. Haec mutatam confirmat, & ut recte agat efficit.
latin.2410: XXI. Sic etiam Petrus Martyr loco saepius memorato dicit gratiam operantem esse quae ab initio voluntatem nostram sanat & immutat: cooperantem vero quae efficit ut ea immutata & sanata recte agat. Quibus addit gratiam operantem & cooperantem esse unam gratiam non duas. Hujus autem variae denominationis rationem esse docet, quod voluntas quum primum sanatur concurrit cum gratia passive. Nam, inquit, ea immutari dicitur, & nos dicimur regenerari. Postea vero active & passive se habet. Nam a Deo impulsa ipsa quoque vult & eligit.
latin.2411: XXII. Neque tamen vel ille vel alii Reformati negant propterea primum conversionis actum esse actum vitalem, & actionem a facultate illa, quae voluntas in nobis dicitur, elicitam: imo non inficiantur esse actionem liberam, & ex earum numero quae in Scholis humanae vocantur. Hoc solum sibi volunt; quum Deus hominem convertit, primum illud quod gratia in nobis operatur quiddam esse quod liberam hominis motionem ad bonum omnino praevenit. Adeoque non videntur hac in parte Reformati a sanioribus inter Scholasticos dissentire, licet aliis verbis mentem suam exprimant.
latin.2412: XXIII. Admittunt quoque Scholae Reformatae Doctores distinctionem gratiae in praevenientem atque subsequentem, sed non omnes eodem sensu. Aretius vult gratiam praevenientem eandem esse cum gratia operante; & gratiam subsequentem eandem cum cooperante, quod etiam plurimi Scholastici sentiunt. Nam, inquit, gratia praeveniens dicitur, quod voluntatem praeveniat, ut initium conversionis non sit a nobis, sed a Deo miserante: subsequens, quod conversionem consequantur novi motus, & bona opera, quae omnia sine gratia efficere non possumus.
latin.2413: XXIV. Martyr vero vult gratiam modo praevenientem, modo subsequentem dici, quoniam sunt multa & diversa munera, quibus nos ordine quodam ornat misericordia Dei. Ita ut omnis gratia quae prior est, dici possit praeveniens respectu posterioris. Primum enim, inquit, sanatur voluntas; ea sanata incipit bene velle: post quae bene voluerit incipit exequi: deinde in bene agendo perseverat: postremo coronatur. Praevenit ergo gratia voluntatem nostram sanando, eadem sequitur efficiendo ut quae recta sunt placeant. Praevenit ut velimus, subsequitur impellendo ut quae voluimus perficiamus. Praevenit movendo ad bona opera, subsequitur donando perseverantiam. Praevenit perseverantiam largiendo, subsequitur eam coronando.
latin.2414: XXV. Sed praeter solennes illas gratiae divisiones usitatas in Schola Rom. multae sunt a Doctoribus Reformatis excogitatae. Sic Tilenus Dei gratiam distinguit in decernentem atque exequentem. Illa, inquit, denotat aeternum Dei propositum de nobis eligendis ante jacta mundi fundamenta: Ista complectitur totam admirandi hujus mysterii oeconomiam, secundum temporum ac graduum varietatem. De divinae voluntatis nominibus disp. 1. th. 24.

sections.title: Grace mostly means God's favour, sometimes his created gifts
sections.pass_a: THESIS I. According to the common sense of the Doctors of the Reformed School Grace for the most part designates the very love and favour of God by which he follows us undeserving, but sometimes also certain gifts and created effects of it. So Tilenus in the theses on the various names of the divine will, first disputation thesis 20, teaches that the grace of God is taken actively and passively. And the former, he says, signification declares the kind and inclined will of God bestowing all things liberally and freely, not from our merit, or from debt, nay. The latter declares some gift freely given.
pass_b: Thesis I. In the common understanding of the doctors of the Reformed school, grace usually means God's own love and favour, with which he pursues us though we do not deserve it. Sometimes, though, it also means certain created gifts and effects of that favour.

So Tilenus, in the first disputation of his theses on the various names of the divine will (thesis 20), teaches that God's grace is taken both actively and passively. In the first sense, he says, it means God's kind and well-disposed will, which, far from acting out of our merit or as a debt, rather bestows everything generously and freely. In the second it means some gift given freely.

sections.title: Peter Martyr: grace as favour toward the elect, and as the gifts it gives
sections.pass_a: II. And so also Peter Martyr in the commonplaces, The name, he says, of grace is taken in sacred scripture in two ways. First indeed and chiefly it signifies the benevolence of God toward men and the free favour by which he follows the Elect. Then because God affects his Elect with excellent gifts, grace sometimes signifies also those gifts which are conferred on us by God freely. Class 3. place 2. paragr. 7.
pass_b: Thesis II. Peter Martyr says the same in his Commonplaces. The word grace, he writes, is used in two ways in holy scripture. First and chiefly it means God's goodwill toward people and the free favour with which he pursues the elect.
Then, because God endows his elect with outstanding gifts, grace sometimes also means the gifts that God bestows on us freely (class 3, locus 2, paragraph 7).

sections.title: Aretius and Polanus: mercy in God and gifts of the Spirit
sections.pass_a: III. Similarly Aretius in the commonplaces in the twenty-fifth place teaches that the sacred writings, when they speak of grace, first understand by this word the free mercy of God by which he manifests himself in the reconciliation and justification of man. Then by grace they signify also the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which gifts he there acknowledges can rightly be called infused grace. And to the same falls back the distinction of Polanus. The grace of God, he says, is said homonymously, For it is either residing in God, or given by God. In the Syntagma of Christian Theology part 1. book 2. chap. 21.
pass_b: Thesis III. Likewise Aretius, in locus 25 of his commonplaces, teaches that when scripture speaks of grace, it means by the word first God's free mercy, by which he shows himself in reconciling and justifying a person.

Next, it uses grace for the gifts of the Holy Spirit as well, and he grants there that these gifts may rightly be called infused grace. Polanus's distinction comes to the same thing. The grace of God, he says, is spoken of homonymously, that is, in two senses: it is either grace that resides in God or grace given by God (Syntagma of Christian Theology, part 1, book 2, chapter 21).

sections.title: Polanus: saving grace is not anything created in us
sections.pass_a: IV. But although Reformed Theologians acknowledge that by the grace of God in sacred scripture are sometimes designated the gifts and effects of divine favour and love toward us, yet they think that in few places grace is to be taken in that sense. Since they contend that all those places where we are said to be by the grace of God elected, called, justified, saved, are by no means to be expounded of some gift inhering in us, but only of the free love and benevolence of God. As especially is to be seen in Polanus. Grace, he says, making pleasing and accepted to God, and so also saving grace, by which we are elected in Christ to eternal salvation, efficaciously called, justified, regenerated, by which finally we are eternally saved, is not a quality infused into us, not something created and inhering in us, not the charity by which we love God, or any other virtue in us. Syntagma Theologicum book 2. chap. 21. just cited.
pass_b: Thesis IV. The Reformed theologians do grant that in holy scripture the grace of God sometimes means the gifts and effects of God's favour and love toward us. Still, they think grace is to be taken that way in only a few places.

For they hold that every passage saying we are chosen, called, justified or saved by God's grace must not be explained of some gift that inheres in us. These passages refer only to God's free love and goodwill. This can be seen especially in Polanus.

Grace that makes us pleasing and acceptable to God, he writes, and so saving grace as well, by which we are chosen in Christ for eternal salvation, effectually called, justified and regenerated, and by which in the end we are saved forever, is not a quality infused into us. It is not something created and inhering in us, not the love with which we love God, nor any other virtue in us (Syntagma, book 2, chapter 21, cited just above).

sections.title: Tilenus: natural and supernatural gifts; gifts for one's own salvation and for the Church
sections.pass_a: V. Further when grace is taken for the gifts and effects of divine favour Tilenus observes that it by a certain common signification embraces nature itself, and its endowments and gifts, yet properly is restricted to certain supernatural gifts granted to men by God. Which gifts again he will have to be of two kinds. For some properly and directly regard the salvation of him who receives, as effects of that active grace by which God justifies us: Such are faith and charity and hope. But others pertain not so much to the particular salvation of those to whom they are given, as to the common use and edification of the whole Church: such are the gift of prophecy, of tongues and of miracles and those which are of this kind.
pass_b: Thesis V. Tilenus also notes that when grace is taken for the gifts and effects of God's favour, in a broad sense it covers nature itself together with its endowments and gifts. Properly, though, it is limited to certain supernatural gifts that God grants to people.

He holds that these gifts are in turn of two kinds. Some bear properly and directly on the salvation of the one who receives them, as effects of that active grace by which God justifies us; faith, love and hope are of this kind. Others concern not so much the personal salvation of those who receive them as the common use and building up of the whole Church, such as the gifts of prophecy, tongues and miracles and others like them.

sections.title: These divisions match the scholastic pair, yet the Reformed fault it
sections.pass_a: VIII. But these divisions of the gifts of grace received among the Reformed differ little or nothing from the solemn division among the Scholastics of grace into grace freely given and grace making pleasing: as Tilenus acknowledges in the before cited first disputation on the various names of the divine will thesis 22. But yet most Reformed Theologians carp at and reprehend that distinction of the Roman School. And first indeed it displeases them that certain gifts of God are specially called grace freely given: because there is no grace which is not given freely. Nor are hope, faith and charity less free gifts of God, than the gift of prophecy, of healings and the like.
pass_b: Thesis VIII. These divisions of the gifts of grace accepted among the Reformed differ little or not at all from the scholastics' standard division of grace into grace freely given and grace that makes pleasing. Tilenus admits as much in thesis 22 of the first disputation on the various names of the divine will, cited above.

Even so, most Reformed theologians criticize and find fault with this distinction of the Roman school. First, they object that some of God's gifts are singled out and called grace freely given, since there is no grace that is not given freely. Hope, faith and love are no less God's free gifts than the gift of prophecy, of healing and the like.

sections.title: Second objection: no created gift first wins God's favour
sections.pass_a: IX. Next it is not approved by them that anything created and inhering in us be called grace making pleasing and accepted to God, as is to be seen in Polanus Aretius and Peter Martyr in the places cited above. Not that they deny that the gifts of God, which the Doctors of the Rom. School designate by grace making pleasing, are something pleasing to God, in which God delights, and which is pleasing to him: But that by these gifts the favour of God is not first won for men; since they themselves are effects of divine favour and love, and proceed from God favouring us, and loving us, even before we received them: according to that of John, Not that we loved God, but because he first loved us.
pass_b: Thesis IX. Second, they do not accept that anything created and inhering in us should be called grace that makes us pleasing and acceptable to God, as can be seen in Polanus, Aretius and Peter Martyr at the places cited above.

They do not deny that the gifts which the doctors of the Roman school mean by grace that makes pleasing are something that pleases God, something he delights in and finds acceptable. Their point is that these gifts are not what first wins God's favour for people. The gifts are themselves effects of God's favour and love, and they come from God already favouring and loving us even before we received them. As John says: not that we loved God, but because he first loved us.

sections.title: Peter Martyr's own words against habitual grace that makes pleasing
sections.pass_a: X. But that this is the opinion of those Doctors is plain from their own words. For thus Peter Martyr in the commonplaces Class three place two number eight speaking of the infused grace of the Scholastics, It is no small error, he says, that they will that we are rendered pleasing to God by this habit, or creature. For it is necessary, when he has affected us with a gift of this kind, that he loved us before. For the love of God precedes all his gifts: And at number thirteen. Nor do they err less, he says, who prate in the schools, that grace freely given is one, grace making pleasing another. For all grace must be given freely. For otherwise, as Paul says, it would not be grace. And since by grace making pleasing they understand a habit, as we taught above, men wrongly determine that by gifts of this kind they are made pleasing before God. For with him by his mercy alone, and for Christ's sake we are received into favour.
pass_b: Thesis X. That this is what those doctors hold is clear from their own words. Peter Martyr, in his Commonplaces (class 3, locus 2, paragraph 8), speaking of the scholastics' infused grace, writes: It is no small error that they want us to be made pleasing to God by this habit or created thing. When he has endowed us with such a gift, he must have loved us first, for God's love comes before all his gifts.

And in paragraph 13 he says: Those who chatter in the schools that grace freely given is one thing and grace that makes pleasing another are just as wrong. All grace has to be given freely, for otherwise, as Paul says, it would not be grace. And since by grace that makes pleasing they mean a habit, as we showed above, they are wrong to lay down that people become pleasing to God through such gifts. With him we are received into favour by his mercy alone and for Christ's sake.

sections.title: Cameron: love for the gifts is human; God's love makes the gifts
sections.pass_a: XI. And similarly Cameron in the digression on grace already mentioned above, But, he says, it is to be observed that the gifts of God are never called grace in this sense, as though by them the favour of God were won, and those gifts rendered us pleasing and accepted to God. But if ever the gifts of God are called grace in this sense, account is had of men, who are induced into love by those gifts, but account is not had of God. That this may be perceived it is to be understood that human love which is won by those gifts, does not make these gifts, but finds them. But divine love the same both found and made these gifts: as a painter who delights in his work, the same rejoices in the beauty of the work, and was the author of that beauty. Therefore no grace ought to have been called making pleasing properly speaking, but rather that ought to have been called the grace of one making pleasing.
pass_b: Thesis XI. Cameron says much the same in the digression on grace mentioned above. It must be noted, he writes, that God's gifts are never called grace in the sense that they win God's favour, as if those gifts made us pleasing and acceptable to God.

If God's gifts are ever called grace in that sense, the reference is to human beings, who are drawn to love by such gifts, and not to God. To see this, one must understand that human love won by these gifts does not make the gifts but finds them. Divine love both found and made them, like a painter who delights in his work: he takes joy in its beauty and was also the one who produced that beauty.
So, strictly speaking, no grace should have been called grace that makes pleasing. It should rather have been called the grace of the one who makes pleasing.

sections.title: Testard: grace freely given invites; grace that makes pleasing transforms
sections.pass_a: XIV. Some also of the Doctors of the Reformed School admit indeed the distinction of grace into freely given and making pleasing, but in another sense, than that which is received among the Scholastic Doctors. For Testard in the Irenicum by grace freely given understands that by which God invites man to salvation: but by grace making pleasing, that by which God efficaciously changes, converts and sanctifies man. Or grace freely given is to him a certain genus; but grace making pleasing that species of that genus by which faith is engendered in man, sins are remitted, holiness is infused. As is to be seen in thesis three hundred. The distinction, he says, of grace into freely given, and making pleasing can be admitted thus, that that be called freely given which only goes before by inviting on God's part, such as is the general: making pleasing, which also is freely given, but by efficaciously changing man, from one to be abhorred makes him pleasing and accepted to God. Or that grace freely given be the most general genus of grace and signify all grace; but grace making pleasing be that species of grace freely given, by which it engenders faith, remits sins, sanctifies, in one word prepares the subject.
pass_b: Thesis XIV. Some doctors of the Reformed school do accept the distinction of grace into grace freely given and grace that makes pleasing, but in a different sense from the one the scholastic doctors accepted. Testard, in his Irenicum, takes grace freely given to be the grace by which God invites a person to salvation, and grace that makes pleasing to be the grace by which God effectually changes, converts and sanctifies a person.

Alternatively, for him grace freely given is a genus, and grace that makes pleasing is the species of that genus through which faith is produced in a person, sins are forgiven and holiness is infused. This can be seen in thesis 300.

The distinction of grace into grace freely given and grace that makes pleasing, he writes, can be accepted in this way. Grace freely given is the grace that only goes before by inviting on God's side, like general grace. Grace that makes pleasing, which is also freely given, effectually changes a person and turns someone abhorrent into someone pleasing and acceptable to God. Or else grace freely given is the most general genus of grace and covers every grace, while grace that makes pleasing is the species of it that produces faith, forgives sins and sanctifies; in a word, it prepares the subject.

sections.title: Rivet and Ferry: grace that makes pleasing is God's favour itself
sections.pass_a: XV. But Rivet in the summary of controversies tractate four question two, by grace freely given understands all the gifts of grace; but by grace making pleasing, which he also calls freely giving, he will have understood the very favour of God, from which those gifts proceed. For by grace making pleasing he signifies grace immanent in God, which does not posit anything about the one favoured, but is the very love of God: but under grace freely given he comprehends all the benefits of calling, justification, &c. flowing down upon us from grace freely giving, as from a most abundant fountain.
pass_b: Thesis XV. Rivet, however, in his Summary of Controversies (tractate 4, question 2), takes grace freely given to mean all the gifts of grace. By grace that makes pleasing, which he also calls grace that gives freely, he means God's favour itself, from which those gifts come.

Paul Ferry uses the same distinction in this sense in chapter 30 of his Specimen of an Orthodox Scholastic. By grace that makes pleasing he means grace that remains within God, which places nothing in the one who is favoured but is simply God's love. Under grace freely given he includes all the benefits of calling, justification and so on, which flow down to us from the grace that gives freely as from an overflowing spring.

sections.title: Actual and habitual grace: older Reformed reject, later ones accept
sections.pass_a: XVI. Further among most Reformed Doctors there is not found expressly set down the distinction of grace into actual and habitual. Nay certain older ones of the Reformed seem to repudiate it. For Peter Martyr in the place cited above professedly refutes the opinion of the Scholastics, who feigned, as he says, that grace is a habit infused into the soul. But the more recent Doctors of the Reformed School, as also most of the old ones, acknowledge that there is given a certain habitual grace. For they speak of the Theological virtues as of habits divinely infused. And Robert Baron a Scot professor of Theology in the Academy of Aberdeen testifies that in this part the consensus of the Moderns, as he speaks, Theologians is unanimous. And also this opinion on habitual grace William Ames defends at length against Grevinchovius in the rescript to the response of Nicolaus Grevinchovius chapter ten.
pass_b: Thesis XVI. Most Reformed doctors do not explicitly state a distinction of grace into actual and habitual. Indeed some of the older Reformed seem to reject it: Peter Martyr, at the place cited above, sets out to refute the scholastics, who imagined, as he puts it, that grace is a habit infused into the soul.

But the more recent doctors of the Reformed school, like most of the older ones too, acknowledge that there is a habitual grace. They speak of the theological virtues as habits infused by God. Robert Baron, a Scot and professor of theology at the University of Aberdeen, testifies that on this point the consensus of the modern theologians, as he calls them, is unanimous. William Ames also defends this view of habitual grace at length against Grevinchovius in chapter 10 of his reply to Nicolaus Grevinchovius's response.

sections.title: The older Reformed meant justifying grace only
sections.pass_a: XVII. Nay those very ones from the older who seem to dissent, I think in reality do not dissent. For when against the Scholastics they contend that grace is not a habit infused into the soul, they manifestly treat of justifying grace. Therefore their mind is not simply, that no habits of virtues are infused into the souls of the faithful by God through the Holy Spirit, and that habits of this kind are nowhere designated by the name of grace: but this only, that grace through which in the scriptures we are said to be saved and justified, in no way consists in those holy habits: but that by that grace is solely signified the mercy and benevolence of God. Of which thing the argument is, that sometimes the grace by which we are saved, justified, nay and regenerated, they not only deny to be a habit and infused quality, but anything created and inhering in us, as we related above of Polanus. And yet the same Polanus in the same chapter acknowledges that there is a certain inhering grace, which, he says, is both faith, and the grace of conversion and regeneration, which they call the grace of Christ the Redeemer, likewise Christian grace. And so when he denies that regenerating grace is anything created and inhering in us, he speaks only of the efficient and impulsive cause of our regeneration, not of the cause which the Scholastics call formal.
pass_b: Thesis XVII. Indeed, I think that even those older writers who seem to disagree do not really disagree. When they argue against the scholastics that grace is not a habit infused into the soul, they are plainly dealing with justifying grace.

So their meaning is not, without qualification, that God infuses no habits of virtue into believers' souls through the Holy Spirit, or that such habits are never called grace. They mean only that the grace by which scripture says we are saved and justified does not consist in those holy habits at all, and that this grace means God's mercy and goodwill alone.

The proof is this. At times they deny that the grace by which we are saved, justified and even regenerated is a habit and infused quality, and they also deny that it is anything created and inhering in us, as we reported of Polanus above. Yet Polanus himself, in the same chapter, grants that there is an inhering grace. This, he says, is faith and also the grace of conversion and regeneration, which people call the grace of Christ the Redeemer, and likewise Christian grace.

So when he denies that regenerating grace is anything created and inhering in us, he is speaking only of the efficient and impelling cause of our regeneration, not of what the scholastics call its formal cause.

sections.title: Habitual grace in the soul's essence: Ferry admits it
sections.pass_a: XVIII. But whether besides the habits of the virtues there is given a certain habitual grace immediately penetrating and affecting the very essence of the soul, as many of the Scholastics opine, is a matter of which most doctors of the Reformed School do not expressly treat, but from which that new and supernatural being, and habitual innovation of all the faculties, which they acknowledge is bestowed on man in regeneration, seems not to be far distant. Paul Ferry however Pastor of the Church of Metz lately deceased in the Lord expressly admits a certain grace of this kind. And he thinks that before the very act of conversion, a certain habitual grace is infused by God into the very substance of the soul, which penetrates the whole soul like a certain spiritual light, and from the substance of the soul insinuates itself into all its faculties: And thus prepares them that they follow the leading of efficacious grace, and obey it easily and spontaneously, as is to be seen in that homily which he published publicly on Heb. 12. 28. But I know that this opinion does not please many.
pass_b: Thesis XVIII. Many scholastics hold that, besides the habits of the virtues, there is a habitual grace that directly penetrates and affects the very essence of the soul. Most doctors of the Reformed school do not deal with this question explicitly. Yet it seems not far from what they do acknowledge, namely the new and supernatural being and the habitual renewal of all the faculties that are given to a person in regeneration.

Paul Ferry, however, pastor of the church at Metz, who recently died in the Lord, explicitly admits a grace of this kind. He holds that before the act of conversion itself God infuses into the very substance of the soul a habitual grace. It pervades the whole soul like a spiritual light and from the soul's substance works its way into all its faculties.

In this way it prepares them to follow the leading of efficacious grace and to obey it readily and willingly, as can be seen in the homily on Hebrews 12:28 that he published. But I know that many people dislike this view.

sections.title: Operating and cooperating grace, taken with the later Thomists
sections.pass_a: XX. However the Doctors of the Reformed School do not disapprove that the Scholastics distinguish grace into Operating and cooperating. But with the more recent Thomists they will have understood by Operating grace that by which someone is first converted to God: but by cooperating that by which someone already converted to God is moved to acting well. Thus Aretius in the place cited above, Grace, he says, is at one time operating, at another cooperating. The former is said to heal our will and change it for the better. The latter confirms it changed, and effects that it act rightly.
pass_b: Thesis XX. The doctors of the Reformed school do not object to the scholastics' distinction of grace into operating and cooperating grace. But, with the more recent Thomists, they take operating grace to be the grace by which a person is first converted to God, and cooperating grace to be the grace by which someone already converted to God is moved to act well.

So Aretius, at the place cited above: Grace, he says, is sometimes operating and sometimes cooperating. The first is said to heal our will and change it for the better; the second strengthens the will once changed and brings it about that it acts rightly.

sections.title: Martyr: one grace, passive at first, then active and passive
sections.pass_a: XXI. Thus also Peter Martyr in the place often mentioned says that operating grace is that which from the beginning heals and changes our will: but cooperating that which effects that it changed and healed act rightly. To which he adds that operating and cooperating grace are one grace not two. But he teaches that the reason of this varied denomination is, that the will when it is first healed concurs with grace passively. For, he says, it is said to be changed, and we are said to be regenerated. But afterwards it holds itself actively and passively. For impelled by God it itself also wills and chooses.
pass_b: Thesis XXI. Peter Martyr likewise, at the place mentioned several times, says that operating grace is the grace that heals and changes our will at the start, and cooperating grace is the grace that makes the will, once changed and healed, act rightly. He adds that operating and cooperating grace are one grace, not two.

He explains that the two names arise because the will, when it is first healed, concurs with grace passively. For, he says, it is said to be changed, and we are said to be regenerated. Afterwards it is both active and passive, because, moved by God, it too wills and chooses.

sections.title: Yet the first act of conversion is vital and free
sections.pass_a: XXII. Nor yet does either he or other Reformed deny on that account that the first act of conversion is a vital act, and an action elicited from that faculty, which is called the will in us: nay they do not deny that it is a free action, and of the number of those which in the Schools are called human. This only they mean; when God converts man, that first thing which grace works in us is something which wholly goes before the free motion of man toward good. And so in this part the Reformed do not seem to dissent from the sounder among the Scholastics, although they express their mind in other words.
pass_b: Thesis XXII. Still, neither he nor the other Reformed deny on this account that the first act of conversion is a vital act, an action produced by the faculty in us called the will. Indeed they do not deny that it is a free action and one of those the schools call human acts.

Their only point is this: when God converts a person, the first thing grace works in us is something that goes entirely before the person's free movement toward good. On this point, then, the Reformed seem not to differ from the sounder scholastics, though they put their meaning in other words.

sections.title: Prevenient and subsequent grace: Aretius
sections.pass_a: XXIII. The Doctors of the Reformed School also admit the distinction of grace into prevenient and subsequent, but not all in the same sense. Aretius will have prevenient grace to be the same with operating grace; and subsequent grace the same with cooperating, which also very many Scholastics think. For, he says, grace is called prevenient, because it goes before the will, that the beginning of conversion be not from us, but from God having mercy: subsequent, because new motions follow conversion, and good works, all which we cannot effect without grace.
pass_b: Thesis XXIII. The doctors of the Reformed school also accept the distinction of grace into prevenient and subsequent, though not all in the same sense. Aretius holds that prevenient grace is the same as operating grace, and subsequent grace the same as cooperating grace, as a great many scholastics also hold.

Grace is called prevenient, he says, because it goes before the will, so that the beginning of conversion is not from us but from God in his mercy. It is called subsequent because new impulses and good works follow conversion, and we cannot do any of these without grace.

sections.title: Martyr: each grace goes before the next and follows the last
sections.pass_a: XXIV. But Martyr will have grace called now prevenient, now subsequent, because there are many and diverse gifts, with which the mercy of God adorns us in a certain order. So that every grace which is prior, can be called prevenient in respect of the posterior. For first, he says, the will is healed; it healed begins to will well: after it has willed well it begins to execute: then in acting well it perseveres: lastly it is crowned. Grace therefore goes before our will by healing, the same follows by effecting that the things which are right please. It goes before that we will, it follows by impelling that we accomplish what we willed. It goes before by moving to good works, it follows by giving perseverance. It goes before perseverance by bestowing, it follows it by crowning.
pass_b: Thesis XXIV. Martyr, on the other hand, holds that grace is called now prevenient and now subsequent because God's mercy adorns us in a certain order with many different gifts. So any grace that comes earlier can be called prevenient with respect to a later one.
First, he says, the will is healed. Once healed, it begins to will what is good; having willed the good, it begins to carry it out; then it perseveres in doing good; and at last it is crowned.

So grace goes before our will by healing it and follows by making right things pleasing to it. It goes before so that we may will, and follows by driving us to accomplish what we have willed. It goes before by moving us to good works and follows by granting perseverance. It goes before perseverance by bestowing it and follows it by crowning it.

sections.title: New Reformed divisions: Tilenus's decreeing and executing grace
sections.pass_a: XXV. But besides those solemn divisions of grace usual in the Rom. School many have been devised by the Reformed Doctors. Thus Tilenus distinguishes the grace of God into decreeing and executing. The former, he says, denotes the eternal purpose of God concerning electing us before the foundations of the world were laid: The latter embraces the whole economy of this admirable mystery, according to the variety of times and degrees. On the names of the divine will disp. 1. th. 24.
pass_b: Thesis XXV. Besides the standard divisions of grace used in the Roman school, the Reformed doctors have devised many of their own. Tilenus, for example, distinguishes God's grace into decreeing and executing grace.

The first, he says, means God's eternal purpose to choose us before the foundations of the world were laid. The second covers the whole working out of this wonderful mystery through its various times and stages (On the names of the divine will, disputation 1, thesis 24).
